title: The same webhook-and-replay demo works for all 50 leads because the record-layer gap is stack-agnostic
content:
The demo shape recorded for this cohort is a single move repeated against whatever the lead already runs: pick one tool from their published stack, have a webhook or a hook dispatch a typed operation into Powerhouse, then delete the source record and replay it from Powerhouse. The research text is explicit about why this generalises — the demo is stack-agnostic *because the gap is*. What is being demonstrated is not a property of any one product; it is the absence of an append-only, attributed record in the place the source record lived.

That matters because these 50 leads have almost nothing in common at the tooling layer. The published stacks in the source records range across Microsoft, SAP, Salesforce, AWS and IBM at one lead, Peppol plus 200-plus in-house software products at another, an explicitly Java-and-open-source shop at a third, and "stack not verified" at several more. Geographically the group spans NL (13), UK (9), DK (8), ES (6), PT (5), SI (4), DE (3) and BE (1). Because the integration binds to a generic extension point rather than to the semantics of a specific product, the engineering cost of the demo is paid once and the per-lead work collapses to choosing a tool and writing one hook.

The commercial caveat is in the lead metadata rather than the demo text. Of the 50 leads carrying this finding, only three sit at priority 1, six at priority 2 and nine at priority 3; 17 are parked at "4 · needs OSS screen" and 15 at "9 · do not pitch". A reusable demo therefore lowers the cost of serving this cohort but does not qualify it — 29 of the 50 arrived from the provisional v2 ranking tail, and the screening work is a separate gate from the build work.

One caveat on the count: row 160 of the group is not a company. It carries the literal values "Organisation" / "Ctry" / "Stack held" — a repeated CSV header row that was imported as a lead — and no source document exists for it in the reactor. The real population behind this finding is 49 companies, which is also what the geographic breakdown above sums to.
